topics.kicker: Shakespeare’s Prince of Denmark · Home of “To be, or not to be”
topics.briefing: When the ghost of his murdered father appears on the castle walls at Elsinore, Prince Hamlet learns that his uncle Claudius is the killer — and spends the rest of _Hamlet_ torn between revenge and doubt. Along the way he delivers the most famous speech in the English language, feigns madness, and loses nearly everyone he loves. Shakespeare’s longest play is also his most quoted, from “to be or not to be” to “something is rotten in the state of Denmark.”

sample.note: the 12 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: Polonius secretly sends a servant named Reynaldo to Paris to spy on his own son. That same scheming advisor is later stabbed through a curtain while eavesdropping on this man and his mother.
tossups.r: This man feigns madness after a ghost reveals that his uncle poisoned his father. He stages a play called _The Murder of Gonzago_ to test his uncle’s guilty conscience. For 10 points, name this Shakespearean prince who wonders “to be or not to be.”

tossups.p: This man’s father appears as a ghost and reveals that the king was poisoned in his ear by his own brother while napping in an orchard, then that brother quickly married the queen. Warned to avenge the murder but “taint not thy mind,” this man swears his friends to secrecy about the apparition.
tossups.r: He later stabs the king’s adviser Polonius through a curtain, mistaking him for his murderous uncle. For 10 points, name this prince who delays avenging his father’s murder throughout a Shakespeare tragedy.

tossups.p: A subplot follows Prince Fortinbras of Norway, who raises an army hoping to win back the lands his father lost to Denmark, mirroring this man’s quest for revenge. Early in the play, this man swears his companions to secrecy after encountering his father’s ghost on the castle battlements.
tossups.r: He later feigns insanity, which he calls putting on an “antic disposition,” to investigate his uncle’s guilt. For 10 points, name this moody prince who delays killing King Claudius for most of a Shakespeare tragedy.

tossups.p: This man tells two old schoolfellows that he has lately lost all his mirth, calling the earth a “sterile promontory” before marveling “what a piece of work is a man.” He later sends those same friends, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, to their deaths in England with a forged letter.
tossups.r: Earlier, this man complains “frailty, thy name is woman” about his mother’s hasty remarriage to his uncle. For 10 points, name this title character who stabs Polonius through a curtain in a Shakespeare tragedy.

tossups.p: After watching a traveling actor weep real tears over a speech about the Trojan queen Hecuba, this man despairs that he, unlike the player, has a real cause for grief yet still fails to act. He resolves to stage a play to “catch the conscience of the king.”
tossups.r: That play, _The Murder of Gonzago_, is nicknamed “the Mousetrap.” For 10 points, name this prince who uses the play to expose his uncle Claudius’s guilt over murdering his father.

tossups.p: Early in the play, the king’s councilor advises his own son, “Neither a borrower nor a lender be,” and later boasts to the king and queen that “brevity is the soul of wit.” That same councilor, Polonius, is stabbed through a curtain by this man.
tossups.r: This man also tells Polonius’s daughter, Ophelia, to “get thee to a nunnery.” For 10 points, name this prince of Denmark who wonders whether “to be or not to be” is the question.

tossups.p: During a heated confrontation with his mother, this man stabs a curtain, killing a hidden eavesdropper he mistook for his uncle. He then drags the body away, later joking that the dead man is “at supper” being eaten by worms.
tossups.r: This man’s accidental victim was Polonius, whose daughter Ophelia later drowns after going mad with grief. For 10 points, name this title prince who avenges his father’s murder in a Shakespeare tragedy.

tossups.p: After this man cruelly tells her to “get thee to a nunnery,” a young noblewoman loses her mind, hands out flowers to the royal court, and drowns after falling from a willow tree into a stream. Her brother Laertes, back from France, plots revenge against this man.
tossups.r: That drowned noblewoman, Ophelia, is mourned in a famous graveyard scene. For 10 points, name this prince who later duels Laertes with a poisoned sword in a Shakespeare tragedy.

tossups.p: In a graveyard, this man picks up the skull of a jester he once knew and sighs “alas, poor Yorick” while calling him “a fellow of infinite jest.” Moments later, he leaps into a freshly dug grave to wrestle with a mourner he accuses of overacting his grief.
tossups.r: That grave belongs to Ophelia, and the mourner is her brother Laertes. For 10 points, name this prince who soon duels Laertes with a poisoned rapier in a Shakespeare tragedy.

tossups.p: A foppish courtier named Osric invites this man to a fencing match that his uncle has secretly rigged with a poisoned blade and a poisoned cup of wine. This man’s mother accidentally drinks from that cup instead, dying before the match ends.
tossups.r: This man then kills Laertes and his uncle Claudius with the same poisoned sword before dying himself. For 10 points, name this title prince whose revenge is completed in the final scene of a Shakespeare tragedy.

tossups.p: Soon after meeting a ghost, this man warns his friends he may start acting strangely, calling it putting on an “antic disposition.” He later rewrites a royal letter so that two old schoolfellows, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, are executed in his place when he is sent to England.
tossups.r: He escapes that voyage after his ship is attacked by pirates. For 10 points, name this prince who returns home to find Ophelia newly buried in a Shakespeare tragedy.

tossups.p: This man claims he could be “bounded in a nutshell” and still count himself “a king of infinite space,” except that he is troubled by bad dreams. He says this to two schoolfellows he suspects the king has sent to spy on him.
tossups.r: Those same friends, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, are later sent to their deaths in England on this man’s forged orders. For 10 points, name this title prince who feigns madness to investigate his father’s murder in a Shakespeare tragedy.

tossups.p: Finding his uncle alone and praying, this man hesitates to kill him, reasoning that a death during prayer might send the murderer’s soul straight to heaven instead of punishing it. He decides to wait for a moment of greater sin.
tossups.r: That hesitation is often cited as proof of this man’s habit of overthinking every decision. For 10 points, name this prince who finally kills his uncle Claudius in the last scene of a Shakespeare tragedy.

tossups.p: This man confronts his mother in her private chamber, comparing his dead father to a god and his new stepfather to “a mildewed ear” blasting his wholesome brother. His father’s ghost appears again during the scene, visible only to this man.
tossups.r: He had just killed Polonius there by stabbing through a curtain. For 10 points, name this prince who rages at his mother, Queen Gertrude, for remarrying so quickly in a Shakespeare tragedy.

tossups.p: This man has more lines than any other Shakespearean character, and in one soliloquy he compares the whole world to an “unweeded garden.” Scholars still debate how much of this man’s famous indecision is genuine and how much is performance.
tossups.r: This man is the title character of Shakespeare’s longest play. For 10 points, name this Prince of Denmark who wonders aloud whether “to be or not to be.”

clues.t: Delivers the famous “to be or not to be” soliloquy while debating whether to go on living

trap.title: Two Hamlets in one play
trap.body: Shakespeare gives the exact same name, Hamlet, to two different characters: the young prince (the answer to this tossup) and his dead father, the murdered king whose ghost walks the battlements. A tossup describing the ghost, the former king, or “the elder Hamlet” is not asking for the title character.
trap.fix: Listen for “Prince,” “young,” or verbs like studies/delays/pretends/stabs — that’s the title character. “King,” “the ghost,” or “the elder” points to his father instead.

topics.name: Oedipus Rex
topics.kicker: Sophocles’ Greek tragic king · Doomed by a prophecy he fled
topics.briefing: An oracle warns Oedipus that he is fated to kill his father and marry his mother, so he flees home to escape it — and ends up doing exactly that without realizing who either person really is. By the time _Oedipus Rex_ begins, he is King of Thebes, famous for solving the Sphinx’s riddle, and determined to find the murderer whose crime has cursed his city. When he discovers that the murderer is himself, he blinds himself in horror.

sample.note: the 12 real QBReader tossups for the Oedipus answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: As an infant, this man is abandoned on Mount Cithaeron with his ankles pinned together, which later gives him his name, meaning “swollen foot.” A shepherd finds and saves him, and he is raised far from home by King Polybus and Queen Merope of Corinth.
tossups.r: Believing them to be his real parents, he later flees Corinth after a prophecy from the oracle at Delphi — and runs straight toward it instead of away. For 10 points, name this Theban king who unknowingly kills his father and marries his mother.

tossups.p: Fleeing a terrible prophecy, this man kills an old traveler and his attendants at a crossroads after a dispute over who must yield the road. He has no idea that the man he just killed was his own father, the king of Thebes.
tossups.r: That king’s death leaves the throne open for this man to inherit after he solves a monster’s riddle. For 10 points, name this legendary Greek king who fulfills a prophecy that he would kill his father and marry his mother.

tossups.p: This man answers “man” when the Sphinx, a winged creature with a lion’s body, asks what walks on four legs at dawn, two legs at midday, and three legs in the evening. Solving that riddle frees the city of Thebes from a curse and wins him the throne.
tossups.r: He soon marries the widowed queen, Jocasta, without realizing she is his own mother. For 10 points, name this king who defeats the Sphinx in a Sophocles tragedy.

tossups.p: A plague strangles the city of Thebes at the start of this man’s story, and he vows to find and punish whoever murdered the previous king to lift the curse. A blind prophet eventually accuses this man himself of being that murderer.
tossups.r: Furious, this man refuses to believe it until the evidence becomes impossible to deny. For 10 points, name this Greek king whose search for a killer ends with the horrifying discovery that he is the killer.

tossups.p: Upon learning the full truth about his marriage, this man takes golden pins from his wife’s robe and blinds himself with them rather than look at his own children any longer. His wife has already hanged herself in her bedroom by the time he does this.
tossups.r: He then asks to be exiled from the city he once saved from the Sphinx. For 10 points, name this self-blinded Theban king of a Sophocles tragedy.

tossups.p: This man’s two sons later kill each other in single combat while fighting over which of them should rule Thebes. Their sister afterward defies a royal order by giving burial rites to the brother branded a traitor.
tossups.r: That same sister, Antigone, had earlier guided this man into exile after he blinded himself. For 10 points, name this disgraced former king whose sons’ feud is chronicled in a related Sophocles tragedy.

tossups.p: In a later play, this man dies peacefully near a grove sacred to the Furies at a town called Colonus, comforted in his final moments by the Athenian king Theseus. Thunder sent by Zeus signals that the moment of his death has come.
tossups.r: His daughter Antigone had guided his wanderings as a blind, exiled beggar for years before this. For 10 points, name this former king of Thebes, whose family’s story is told in the three Theban plays of Sophocles.

tossups.p: A Roman playwright named Seneca the Younger also wrote a tragedy about this same cursed king, opening with a terrible plague over Thebes. This man’s Greek legend was far older, though, stretching back to Homer, who already mentions his fate briefly in the _Odyssey_.
tossups.r: Centuries later, Sophocles turned his story into one of ancient Greece’s most famous tragedies. For 10 points, name this king who kills his father and marries his mother without knowing either fact.

tossups.p: Before this man is even born, an oracle warns his father, King Laius, that his own son will someday kill him. Terrified, Laius has the infant’s feet pierced and left on a mountainside to die, a plan that fails when a kind shepherd intervenes.
tossups.r: Years later, that abandoned son unknowingly fulfills the very prophecy his father tried to prevent. For 10 points, name this Theban king who kills Laius without recognizing him.

tossups.p: A messenger from Corinth arrives to report a king’s death, expecting this man to feel relief — instead, the messenger’s news that this man was merely adopted sets off a chain of discoveries that destroys him. An old shepherd is then summoned to confirm the messenger’s story.
tossups.r: That shepherd reveals he once saved an abandoned baby with pinned feet on Mount Cithaeron. For 10 points, name this man who learns from that shepherd the horrifying truth about his own birth.

tossups.p: This man’s wife hangs herself inside the palace once she realizes that her husband is also her own son. A palace servant later reports that this man found her body and then blinded himself in grief and horror.
tossups.r: That wife and mother was named Jocasta. For 10 points, name this Theban king whose family tragedy is the subject of a Sophocles play.

tossups.p: This man’s story became the basis for a theory Sigmund Freud later named after him, even though Freud’s psychological theory and this man’s actual myth are two very different things. Aristotle praised the play about this man as the finest example of tragedy in his work _Poetics_.
tossups.r: Sophocles wrote three separate plays about this man and his family. For 10 points, name this cursed Theban king, the subject of ancient Greece’s most studied tragedy.

tossups.p: This man’s name comes from Greek words meaning “swollen foot,” a reference to an injury from early in his life. As an adult, his ankles still bear the scars of that old wound.
tossups.r: Those scars come from having his ankles pinned together when he was left on a mountain as an infant. For 10 points, name this king whose very name hints at his unusual origin.

tossups.p: This man arrives in Thebes as a stranger, solves the riddle that has been killing anyone who fails it, and is rewarded with both the throne and the recently widowed queen’s hand in marriage. He has no idea that the queen and the throne are both connected to his own hidden past.
tossups.r: That queen, Jocasta, turns out to be his biological mother. For 10 points, name this unwitting king of a Sophocles tragedy.

tossups.p: After blinding himself, this man asks his brother-in-law to take over as ruler and to care for his daughters. That brother-in-law, Creon, later rules Thebes as the stern king in _Antigone_.
tossups.r: This man eventually leaves Thebes to wander as a blind beggar guided by his daughter Antigone. For 10 points, name this once-mighty king brought down by a prophecy he could not escape.

trap.title: The myth, not the complex
trap.body: Sigmund Freud borrowed this character’s name for his “Oedipus complex” theory about unconscious desire — but a Literature question wants the Greek tragic hero, not the psychology term. His wife Jocasta, his brother-in-law (and uncle) Creon, and his daughter Antigone are also NOT the answer, even though clues about them lead into it.
trap.fix: If the clues mention a prophecy, a crossroads killing, a riddle about the Sphinx, or self-blinding, the answer is the king himself, not whoever surrounds him.

topics.name: Macbeth
topics.kicker: Shakespeare’s “Scottish play” · A prophecy-driven spiral into murder
topics.briefing: Three witches greet the Scottish general Macbeth with a prophecy that he will become king — so he and his wife murder their way to the throne to make it happen. Guilt haunts them both: she sleepwalks, scrubbing at invisible blood on her hands, while he sees the ghost of the friend he had killed. Shakespeare’s shortest tragedy is so famously cursed that actors avoid saying its name backstage, calling it “the Scottish play” instead.

sample.note: 8 of the 10 real QBReader results for “Macbeth” (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked); 1 off-topic “ghosts” tossup and 1 separate “Lady Macbeth” tossup were set aside

tossups.p: The previous Thane of Cawdor is sentenced to death for treason just before three witches hail this general with that exact title, along with Thane of Glamis and “king hereafter.” His friend Banquo receives a stranger prophecy: that his own descendants, not this man’s, will someday be kings.
tossups.r: Urged on by his wife, this man murders King Duncan that same night to make the prophecy come true. For 10 points, name this Scottish general who seizes the throne in a Shakespeare tragedy nicknamed “the Scottish play.”

tossups.p: On his way to commit his first murder, this man hallucinates a bloody dagger floating in midair, calling it “a dagger of the mind.” Earlier, three witches had hailed him as a future king.
tossups.r: Soon afterward, this man murders King Duncan in his sleep. For 10 points, name this Scottish thane whose wife eggs him on toward murder in a Shakespeare tragedy.

tossups.p: At this general’s castle in Inverness, Lennox and a nobleman from Fife arrive together, interrupting this man’s guilty brooding the morning after a killing. Earlier, this man worried aloud that he had only “vaulting ambition” to justify what he was about to do.
tossups.r: He blames the murder on two drunken guards, whom he then kills to silence. For 10 points, name this Scottish general who takes King Duncan’s throne in a Shakespeare tragedy.

tossups.p: This man’s wife begs evil spirits to “unsex” her and fill her with cruelty before their first crime together. Later, guilt drives that same woman to sleepwalk through the castle, scrubbing at hands she imagines are stained with blood.
tossups.r: She finally mutters “out, damned spot!” while a doctor and a gentlewoman watch helplessly. For 10 points, name this general whose wife’s guilt unravels as badly as his own in a Shakespeare tragedy.

tossups.p: At a banquet celebrating his new throne, this man sees the bloody ghost of a murdered friend sitting in his own chair, though no one else at the table can see it. He had ordered that friend killed out of fear of a witches’ prophecy about royal descendants.
tossups.r: That murdered friend was Banquo. For 10 points, name this Scottish king who nearly loses his composure at a feast in a Shakespeare tragedy.

tossups.p: A seemingly impossible prophecy — that he cannot be defeated until Great Birnam Wood marches to Dunsinane Hill — comes true when an enemy army cuts branches to disguise their approach. This man has grown so confident in his safety that he dismisses the first report of it as a lie.
tossups.r: That same army includes a nobleman whose family this man had murdered. For 10 points, name this Scottish king who is finally killed by Macduff in a Shakespeare tragedy.

tossups.p: Three witches promise this man that “none of woman born” shall ever harm him, giving him false confidence in his final battle. That prophecy collapses when his enemy reveals he was “from his mother’s womb untimely ripped,” meaning he was born by what we would now call a cesarean section.
tossups.r: That enemy, Macduff, kills this man in single combat. For 10 points, name this title tyrant of a Shakespeare tragedy nicknamed “the Scottish play.”

tossups.p: On learning of his wife’s death, this man delivers a bleak speech calling life “a walking shadow” and a “poor player” who struts and frets upon a stage. That speech famously repeats “tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow.”
tossups.r: Moments later, he learns that Great Birnam Wood is marching toward his castle at Dunsinane. For 10 points, name this Scottish general whose murderous rise is undone by prophecy in a Shakespeare tragedy.

tossups.p: Three ghostly apparitions — a floating armored head, a bloody child, and a crowned child holding a tree — give this man a set of riddling warnings during a second visit to the witches. He takes the last two as promises of safety.
tossups.r: Those apparitions warn him about Macduff, about being born of woman, and about Birnam Wood. For 10 points, name this Scottish general who is doomed by misreading the apparitions’ prophecies in a Shakespeare tragedy.

tossups.p: A young J. R. R. Tolkien was so disappointed that this play’s army-disguised-as-a-forest trick turned out to be just soldiers carrying branches that he later invented walking, talking tree-creatures called Ents for his own fiction. That disguised army was marching on this man’s castle at Dunsinane.
tossups.r: The trick fulfilled a prophecy about Great Birnam Wood. For 10 points, name this Scottish king of a Shakespeare tragedy who is undone by that very prophecy.

tossups.p: Before their first crime, this man’s wife tells him to “screw your courage to the sticking place” and mocks his hesitation as unmanly. She had earlier read a letter in which this man described meeting three witches on a heath.
tossups.r: That same night, he murders King Duncan while the king is a guest in his own castle. For 10 points, name this Scottish thane who rises to the throne through murder in a Shakespeare tragedy.

tossups.p: Three witches chant “double, double, toil and trouble” while brewing a potion with eye of newt and toe of frog for this man’s second visit to their cave. He demands to know his fate even though the witches warn him it will only harm him to hear it.
tossups.r: Their apparitions wrongly convince him that he is invincible. For 10 points, name this Scottish general who receives three fatal prophecies in a Shakespeare tragedy.

tossups.p: Fearing a prophecy that a murdered friend’s descendants will rule instead of his own, this man hires assassins to kill that friend and his young son on a dark road. The son, Fleance, escapes into the night.
tossups.r: That murdered friend’s ghost later haunts a royal banquet. For 10 points, name this Scottish king who orders Banquo’s murder in a Shakespeare tragedy.

tossups.p: This man stares at his blood-soaked hands after a killing and wonders if “all great Neptune’s ocean” could ever wash them clean. He and his wife frame two drunken guards for the crime by planting bloody daggers on them.
tossups.r: The victim, King Duncan, had been a guest under this man’s own roof that night. For 10 points, name this Scottish general whose wife says after the deed that “a little water clears us of this deed.”

tossups.p: This man’s entire downfall is driven by three prophecies from three witches, each of which comes true in a way he never expects. Shakespeare based this man’s story loosely on a real medieval Scottish king described in Holinshed’s _Chronicles_.
tossups.r: The real history is far less dramatic than the play’s murders, ghosts, and sleepwalking. For 10 points, name this title general of Shakespeare’s shortest tragedy, nicknamed “the Scottish play.”

topics.briefing: The _Iliad_ is Homer’s epic poem about a few weeks in the final year of a ten-year Greek siege of Troy. It opens with the hero Achilles raging at his commander Agamemnon, and it ends with the Trojan king Priam ransoming the body of his son Hector, whom Achilles has killed. Along the way the gods take sides, armies clash outside the city walls, and Achilles loses his dearest companion, Patroclus.

tossups.p: In this epic, Zeus’s mortal son Sarpedon falls to Patroclus’s spear, and the grieving king of the gods weeps tears of blood. Earlier in the same work, Achilles’s mother Thetis, a sea nymph, convinces Zeus to let the Trojans win while her son sits out the fighting.

tossups.p: Agamemnon dispatches Odysseus and Ajax to offer this poem’s central hero rich gifts and the return of a captured woman, but the sulking warrior turns them down flat. Earlier in the same poem, Paris briefly duels Menelaus one-on-one until Aphrodite spirits the overmatched Trojan prince away.
tossups.r: Helen herself names the Greek champions from atop Troy’s walls for old King Priam. For 10 points, identify this epic that climaxes with Hector’s death and Priam’s ransom of his son’s body.

tossups.p: In this work, a priest named Chryses prays to Apollo for a plague after Agamemnon refuses to free his captured daughter, Chryseis. That same quarrel over captive women also costs the hero Achilles his prize, Briseis, pushing him to withdraw from battle.
tossups.r: Hector’s wife Andromache and infant son Astyanax say a tearful goodbye to him atop the walls of Troy in this poem. For 10 points, name this poem that ends with Priam ransoming his son Hector’s corpse from Achilles.

tossups.r: Near the end, funeral games featuring a chariot race honor the hero’s fallen companion. For 10 points, name this Greek epic traditionally credited to Homer.

tossups.p: This poem opens by invoking a Muse to sing of one warrior’s wrath after Agamemnon claims his captive woman, Briseis. Elsewhere in the same work, Zeus’s own son Sarpedon dies fighting on the Trojan side.
tossups.r: That warrior’s companion Patroclus borrows his armor and is killed by Hector while wearing it. For 10 points, name this companion epic to the _Odyssey_.

tossups.p: In this epic, a Trojan archer named Pandarus wounds Menelaus with an arrow during a broken truce, touching off furious fighting. Nestor, the elderly king of Pylos, offers counsel to the Greek commanders throughout this same work.

tossups.r: This work’s war began when Paris carried off Menelaus’s wife, Helen. For 10 points, name this Trojan War epic attributed to Homer.

tossups.p: In this poem, the priest Chryses’s prayers bring a plague down on the Greek camp after his daughter Chryseis is seized by Agamemnon. Odysseus and Ajax later fail to talk this poem’s central hero out of his anger during an embassy bearing gifts.
tossups.r: That hero returns to battle only after his companion Patroclus is killed while wearing his armor. For 10 points, name this epic about Achilles’s rage during the Trojan War.

tossups.p: The funeral games held for a fallen warrior in this poem include a chariot race and other contests. Diomedes, guided by Athena, wounds two different gods on the battlefield of this same work.
tossups.r: This poem’s Catalogue of Ships lists the Greek forces besieging Troy. For 10 points, name this epic poem that ends with Priam ransoming Hector’s body, written by Homer.

tossups.p: Hector’s wife begs him not to return to combat, with their baby son beside her, in a scene from early in this poem. Zeus weeps tears of blood when his own son Sarpedon dies in this poem’s fighting.
tossups.r: This poem’s central quarrel begins when Agamemnon takes the captive woman Briseis away from Achilles. For 10 points, name this epic that is a companion piece to the _Odyssey_.

tossups.p: Funeral games for Patroclus, including a chariot race, take place late in this epic poem. Earlier, this poem’s narrative follows the wrath of a hero after Agamemnon dishonors him by seizing his captive, Briseis.
tossups.r: This poem ends after Achilles allows the Trojan king Priam to ransom his son Hector’s corpse. For 10 points, name this epic attributed to Homer and set during the Trojan War.

tossups.p: This poem’s fourth book features the archer Pandarus breaking a truce by wounding Menelaus, while its eighteenth book features Hephaestus forging a new shield for its hero. Nestor, an aging king, counsels the Greeks throughout the fighting in this work.
tossups.r: This poem opens with a quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles over the captive Briseis. For 10 points, name this Greek epic set in the final year of the Trojan War.

tossups.p: After this poem’s hero kills Hector and drags his body behind a chariot, the grieving king Priam travels to ransom his son’s corpse. Earlier in the poem, Thetis asks Zeus to let the Trojans win while her son refuses to fight.

trap.title: No Trojan Horse here
trap.body: Many kids assume the famous Trojan Horse trick happens in the Iliad, but it doesn’t. This poem ends with Hector’s funeral, well before Troy actually falls. The horse shows up only in brief flashbacks in the Odyssey and gets its full telling in Virgil’s Aeneid.
trap.fix: If a clue describes the wooden horse, Sinon’s trick, or the city of Troy actually burning, the answer is the Aeneid (or just “the Trojan War”) — not the Iliad.

topics.briefing: _Moby-Dick_ follows the sailor Ishmael, who signs aboard the whaling ship Pequod under its one-legged captain, Ahab. Ahab turns the voyage away from ordinary whaling and toward revenge against Moby Dick, the giant white whale that bit off his leg on an earlier voyage. Along the way Ishmael bonds with the tattooed harpooner Queequeg, and the voyage builds toward a catastrophic final chase.

tossups.p: This work’s pilgrims gather at London’s Tabard Inn, where some twenty-nine of them agree to a storytelling contest. One tale in this collection follows a knight who must discover what women want most, learning the answer from an old woman he is forced to marry.
tossups.r: That old woman is magically transformed into a beautiful young bride once the knight gives her power in their marriage. For 10 points, name this collection of stories by Geoffrey Chaucer, on the way to the shrine of Thomas Becket.

tossups.p: This work was left unfinished at its author’s death, ending with a long sermon-like tale from the Parson. Its pilgrims represent nearly every rank of medieval society, from a noble knight down to a humble plowman.
tossups.r: Three greedy young men in one of its tales try to kill Death itself and end up killing one another over a pile of gold. For 10 points, name this collection of stories written in Middle English by Geoffrey Chaucer.

tossups.p: This work opens with a famous description of April showers before introducing its travelers one by one. Among those travelers are two nuns and a pardoner whom the text mocks for selling fake religious relics.
tossups.r: One tale in this collection follows a knight who learns what women want most from an old woman he is forced to marry. For 10 points, name this collection of stories told on the road to the shrine of Thomas Becket, written by Geoffrey Chaucer.

tossups.p: This work’s host, Harry Bailey, keeps order among the pilgrims and promises a free dinner to whoever tells the best tale. In one story in this collection, a young scholar tricks a jealous old carpenter into tying three tubs to the ceiling to survive a made-up flood.
tossups.r: In another tale, a knight learns that what women most desire is power over their own marriages. For 10 points, name this collection of stories written in Middle English by Geoffrey Chaucer.

tossups.p: This work’s Knight, the highest-ranking traveler, tells the very first tale after a drawing of lots. That opening tale follows two knights, Palamon and Arcite, who both fall in love with the same woman, Emily.
tossups.r: Later in the collection, a clever rooster named Chauntecleer narrowly escapes a flattering fox. For 10 points, name this collection of stories told by pilgrims traveling toward the shrine of the murdered Archbishop Thomas Becket, written by Geoffrey Chaucer.

tossups.p: This work’s Wife of Bath is described in its opening section as gap-toothed and married five separate times. Elsewhere, its Cook is described as having an unpleasant open sore on his shin, and its Monk is cut off after about seventeen tragic mini-biographies.
tossups.r: The first two details come from this work’s lengthy opening section introducing each pilgrim in turn. For 10 points, name this collection of stories written in Middle English by Geoffrey Chaucer.

tossups.p: This work’s pilgrims agree to a storytelling contest proposed by their host, Harry Bailey, at London’s Tabard Inn. One tale in this collection follows three greedy young men who try to kill Death itself and end up killing each other over gold instead.
tossups.r: Another tale follows a knight who must discover what women want most, eventually marrying an old woman who teaches him the answer. For 10 points, name this collection of stories by Geoffrey Chaucer, on the road to Thomas Becket’s shrine.

tossups.p: This work is written mostly in heroic couplets and was left unfinished, breaking off after a sermon-like tale from the Parson. Its pilgrims range from a noble knight down to a humble plowman, representing nearly every rank of medieval society.
tossups.r: The collection opens with a famous description of April showers before its narrator introduces each traveler in turn. For 10 points, name this work by Geoffrey Chaucer, a collection of stories told on the road to Thomas Becket’s shrine.

clues.t: A collection of stories written in Middle English by Geoffrey Chaucer
Begins when a group of pilgrims gathers at London’s Tabard Inn
Follows pilgrims traveling to the shrine of the murdered Archbishop Thomas Becket
The pilgrims pass the journey by holding a storytelling contest, with a free dinner as the prize
In one tale, a knight must discover what women want most, learning the answer from an old woman he is forced to marry
In one tale, a young scholar tricks a jealous old carpenter into tying three tubs to the ceiling to survive a made-up flood
In one fable-like tale, a clever rooster named Chauntecleer narrowly escapes being eaten by a flattering fox
In one tale, three greedy young men set out to kill Death itself and end up killing each other over a pile of gold
In the opening tale, two knights both fall in love with the same woman, Emily, and compete for her in a tournament
Opens with a famous description of April showers waking up the land before the pilgrims set out
The Knight, the highest-ranking pilgrim, tells the very first tale after a drawing of lots
The Tabard Inn’s host, Harry Bailey, proposes the storytelling contest and judges each tale
The Monk’s rambling string of tragic mini-biographies is cut off by the Knight after about seventeen stories
The Wife of Bath, one of the pilgrims, is described as gap-toothed and has outlived five husbands
The Cook, one of the pilgrims, is described as having an unpleasant open sore on his shin
The narrator counts “nine and twenty” travelers in the group of pilgrims, not including himself
Written mostly in rhyming pairs of lines called heroic couplets, an early use of that form in English
Left unfinished at its author’s death, breaking off after a sermon-like Parson’s Tale and an author’s note of apology
Its pilgrims represent nearly every rank of medieval society, from a noble knight down to a poor plowman
Among the pilgrims traveling together are two nuns and a pardoner whom the text mocks for selling fake religious relics

trap.title: One tale, or the collection?
trap.body: “The Miller’s Tale,” “The Wife of Bath’s Tale,” “The Knight’s Tale,” and “The Pardoner’s Tale” are each their own individual stories inside this work, and full tournaments sometimes ask about them as separate answer lines. A clue about one specific story is not enough by itself — the question has to be asking about the whole frame narrative.
trap.fix: Listen for the overall frame: pilgrims, the Tabard Inn, Harry Bailey, or the journey to the shrine. If the clue only describes events inside one story with no mention of the pilgrims telling it, it may want that tale’s own answer line instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: The Canterbury Tales (accept The Tales of Canterbury).

topics.kicker: Homer’s epic of Odysseus’s trip home · The model for every journey story
topics.briefing: After ten years fighting at Troy, the Greek hero Odysseus faces a trip home just as long: ten more years battling monsters, storms, and a vengeful sea god just to reach his island kingdom of Ithaca. Along the way he outsmarts a one-eyed giant, resists an enchantress’s spells, and plugs his crew’s ears against a deadly song. Homer’s _Odyssey_ turned that voyage into the most famous homecoming story ever told.

qb.tip: Giveaway lines were often cut off by the fetch, but Scylla and Charybdis showed up in almost every sample tossup — it’s the single most reliable stock clue.

sample.note: the 7 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: In this epic, its protagonist pours libations of blood to summon spirits in the underworld, including the prophet Tiresias [“ty-REE-see-us”] and his own mother. A witch on the island of Aeaea [“ay-EE-uh”] sends him there after turning his crew into pigs.
tossups.r: That witch, Circe, is resisted thanks to an herb called moly given to him by Hermes. For 10 points, name this epic poem about a Greek king’s ten-year voyage home from the Trojan War, written by Homer.

tossups.p: Some of this poem’s sailors eat a memory-erasing fruit and have to be dragged back to their ship by force. Cannibal giants called the Laestrygonians [“less-trih-GO-nee-unz”] later hurl boulders that sink all but one of its hero’s ships.
tossups.r: That hero also loses six men to a six-headed monster named Scylla while steering past a whirlpool, Charybdis. For 10 points, name this epic poem about a Greek king’s long voyage home, by Homer.

tossups.p: This poem opens years after the Trojan War with its hero’s son sailing off to question old King Nestor and then Menelaus [“men-uh-LAY-us”] for news of his missing father. Spartan queen Helen, whose kidnapping started that war, appears at Menelaus’s court as well.
tossups.r: That son, Telemachus, later stands beside his disguised father, who strings an old bow and shoots an arrow through twelve axe heads. For 10 points, name this epic in which Telemachus’s father finally comes home to Ithaca.

tossups.p: A nymph named Calypso [“kuh-LIP-so”] keeps this epic’s hero on her island of Ogygia for seven years, offering him immortality if he’ll stay forever. He refuses, builds a raft, and is later shipwrecked near the Phaeacian [“fee-AY-shun”] court.
tossups.r: There, princess Nausicaa [“naw-SIK-ay-uh”] finds him and brings him to her father’s palace, where he tells his whole story so far. For 10 points, name this epic poem by Homer about that storyteller’s trip home from Troy.

tossups.p: This epic’s hero tells a Cyclops his name is “Nobody,” blinds the giant, then escapes his cave by clinging to the underside of sheep. That trick earns the lasting fury of the sea god Poseidon, father of the Cyclops he blinded.
tossups.r: Poseidon then wrecks the hero’s raft just before he reaches the Phaeacians. For 10 points, name this epic poem in which a cunning Greek king battles a one-eyed giant on his way home from the Trojan War.

tossups.p: King Aeolus [“EE-oh-lus”] gives this epic’s hero a bag holding every wind except a favorable one; his crew opens it out of greed just as Ithaca comes into view, blowing them straight back out to sea. Later, the witch Circe turns that crew into pigs.
tossups.r: Circe is resisted with an herb called moly before she becomes a helpful host instead. For 10 points, name this Homeric epic about a king’s ten-year struggle to sail home from Troy.

tossups.p: This poem’s heroine delays a palace full of suitors for years by weaving, then secretly unraveling, a burial shroud meant for her father-in-law Laertes [“lay-ER-teez”]. She finally agrees to marry whoever can string her husband’s massive bow.
tossups.r: That husband, in disguise as a beggar, wins his own contest and then slaughters the suitors with his son’s help. For 10 points, name this epic about Penelope’s long wait for her husband to return from the Trojan War.

tossups.p: An old nurse named Eurycleia [“yur-ih-KLY-uh”] recognizes this epic’s disguised hero by a scar on his leg while washing a beggar’s feet, but he silences her before she can give away the secret. Even his own dog, Argos, recognizes him and then dies of old age.
tossups.r: His wife still isn’t convinced until he describes the bed he built around a living olive tree. For 10 points, name this epic poem about a king’s disguised return to Ithaca.

tossups.p: This epic’s hero disguises himself as a beggar with help from Athena and stays first with a loyal swineherd named Eumaeus [“yoo-MEE-us”]. Years earlier, his remaining crew had been destroyed by one of Zeus’s own thunderbolts.
tossups.r: Zeus punished that crew for eating the sacred cattle of the sun god Helios on the island of Thrinacia [“thrih-NAY-shuh”]. For 10 points, name this Homeric epic in which only its hero survives to reach home.

tossups.p: This epic’s hero ties himself to his ship’s mast and plugs his crew’s ears with beeswax so they can sail safely past a deadly, beautiful song. Shortly after that, the same ship barely escapes a six-headed monster and a ship-swallowing whirlpool in a narrow strait.
tossups.r: That song belongs to the Sirens, who lure sailors to their deaths on rocky shores. For 10 points, name this epic poem about a Greek king’s voyage home from the Trojan War, written by Homer.

tossups.p: A council of gods, minus an angry sea god, decides to finally let this epic’s hero leave the nymph Calypso’s island after seven years. Messenger god Hermes delivers the order, and the hero builds a raft to sail off alone.
tossups.r: Storms sent by that angry sea god, Poseidon, wreck the raft before friendly Phaeacian sailors take him the rest of the way home. For 10 points, name this epic about a king’s ten-year journey back to Ithaca.

tossups.p: This epic’s hero tells much of his own backstory in flashback at a foreign king’s court, describing how cannibal Laestrygonians [“less-trih-GO-nee-unz”] sank eleven of his twelve ships and how a bag of winds blew his fleet off course just before reaching home.
tossups.r: He also recalls resisting a witch’s magic with a protective herb called moly. For 10 points, name this Homeric epic told partly in flashback by its well-traveled Greek hero.

tossups.p: In this epic, the goddess Athena disguises herself as a family friend named Mentor to encourage a young prince to sail out and gather news of his missing father from old war veterans.
tossups.r: That prince, Telemachus, later helps his father fight the suitors crowding his mother’s palace. For 10 points, name this epic about Telemachus’s father’s return from the Trojan War.

tossups.p: Some of this epic’s sailors taste a fruit that erases all memory of home, and their captain has to physically drag them away. Soon after, a one-eyed son of Poseidon traps the same crew inside his cave and eats several of them.
tossups.r: That giant, the Cyclops Polyphemus [“pol-ee-FEE-mus”], is blinded and tricked by a hero who calls himself “Nobody.” For 10 points, name this epic about a Greek king’s long, monster-filled trip home.

tossups.p: At the very end of this epic, the families of the suitors nearly start a civil war on Ithaca before Athena steps in to force a peace. Earlier, the hero reunites with his own elderly father, who is working in an orchard.
tossups.r: That father, Laertes [“lay-ER-teez”], helps fight off the suitors’ relatives one last time. For 10 points, name this epic poem by Homer that ends with a king finally, fully restored to his home in Ithaca.

clues.t: Epic poem by Homer about a Greek king’s ten-year voyage home after the Trojan War
Its hero is the clever king of the small Greek island of Ithaca
Wife Penelope fends off a palace full of suitors who want to marry her and take the throne
Son Telemachus sails off for news of his father, then helps reclaim their palace
Blinds the one-eyed giant Cyclops Polyphemus [“pol-ee-FEE-mus”] to escape his cave
Ties himself to the mast and plugs his crew’s ears with wax to survive the deadly song of the Sirens
The witch Circe turns his crew into pigs; he resists her spell using a protective herb called moly
Must sail between the monster Scylla and the whirlpool Charybdis [“kuh-RIB-dis”], losing six men to Scylla
King Aeolus [“EE-oh-lus”] gives him a bag of winds that his crew foolishly opens near home
Spends seven years on the nymph Calypso’s island of Ogygia, who offers him immortality to stay
Princess Nausicaa [“naw-SIK-ay-uh”] finds him shipwrecked and brings him to her father’s Phaeacian court
Wins a contest by stringing his own great bow and shooting an arrow through twelve axe heads
His old dog, Argos, recognizes him after twenty years away and then dies
His crew is destroyed by one of Zeus’s thunderbolts after eating the sacred cattle of the sun god Helios on the island of Thrinacia [“thrih-NAY-shuh”]
Penelope delays the suitors for years by weaving, then secretly unraveling, a burial shroud for her father-in-law Laertes
The old nurse Eurycleia [“yur-ih-KLY-uh”] recognizes him by a scar on his leg while washing a disguised beggar’s feet
Penelope finally confirms his identity by testing his knowledge of their bed, built around a living olive tree
Tricks the Cyclops by calling himself “Nobody,” then blinds him with a sharpened, fire-hardened stake
Earns the sea god Poseidon’s lasting fury by blinding Poseidon’s own son, the Cyclops, and then boasting about it
Travels to the underworld and pours libations of blood to summon the ghost of the prophet Tiresias [“ty-REE-see-us”]
Some of his men eat the memory-erasing fruit of the Lotus-Eaters and have to be dragged back to the ships
Cannibal giants called the Laestrygonians [“less-trih-GO-nee-unz”] destroy all but one of his ships by hurling boulders
The poem opens years after the Trojan War with his son traveling to question Nestor and Menelaus [“men-uh-LAY-us”] for news of him

trap.title: The poem, or the man?
trap.body: This answer line is the NAME OF THE POEM, not its hero. The hero is Odysseus—whose Latin name, confusingly, is Ulysses. And “Ulysses” is also the title of a completely different (and famously difficult) 1922 novel by James Joyce. Three names, three different correct answers to three different questions.
trap.fix: If the question asks you to “name this epic poem” or “name this work,” the answer is the Odyssey itself. If it asks for the Greek king or hero by name, that’s Odysseus (or Ulysses) — a different answer entirely, and neither one is the James Joyce novel.

topics.name: Paradise Lost
topics.kicker: Milton’s epic of Satan’s fall · Grand English verse without rhyme
topics.briefing: John Milton was completely blind when he dictated this towering poem about the biggest rebellion in history: Satan’s war against God. Told in majestic, unrhymed blank verse, _Paradise Lost_ follows Satan’s fall from Heaven, his scheme to corrupt Adam and Eve, and humanity’s expulsion from the Garden of Eden. Milton said his goal was simply to “justify the ways of God to men.”

qb.tip: Pandemonium and the “better to reign in Hell” line show up constantly — they’re the two most reliable stock clues by far.

sample.note: the 4 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: In this poem, the newly invented weapon of artillery briefly turns the tide of a three-day celestial battle, until the Son of God single-handedly routs the rebel army and drives it over Heaven’s edge. The loyal angel Abdiel stands alone against his former commander beforehand.
tossups.r: That commander, Satan, had convinced a third of Heaven’s angels to revolt with him. For 10 points, name this epic poem about the War in Heaven and the subsequent fall of Adam and Eve, written by John Milton.

tossups.p: In Hell’s new capital, three of this poem’s demons debate strategy: Moloch wants open war again, Belial counsels inaction, and Mammon suggests they simply mine Hell’s gold instead. Their leader ultimately volunteers to scout the newly created universe alone.
tossups.r: That leader travels through the formless realm of Chaos to reach Earth and tempt humanity instead. For 10 points, name this epic poem about Satan’s rebellion and the fall of Adam and Eve, written by John Milton.

tossups.p: Two monstrous gatekeepers named Sin and Death guard the only exit from Hell in this poem, and Sin — who is also this poem’s villain’s own daughter — unlocks the gate to let him through. He then crosses the realm of Chaos to reach a newly created universe.
tossups.r: That villain, Satan, hopes to corrupt God’s newest creation out of pure spite. For 10 points, name this epic poem in which Satan schemes to ruin Adam and Eve.

tossups.p: Disguised as a young cherub, this poem’s villain tricks the sun-angel Uriel into pointing him toward a certain garden, where he later perches on a tree like a cormorant. Uriel soon realizes his mistake and warns the angels guarding that garden.
tossups.r: By then, the villain has already leapt over the garden’s wall like a prowling wolf. For 10 points, name this epic poem in which Satan sneaks into the Garden of Eden.

tossups.p: Angels named Ithuriel and Zephon discover this poem’s villain crouched like a toad at a sleeping woman’s ear, trying to plant a troubling dream in her mind. Confronted, he briefly swells to his true monstrous size before fleeing the garden.
tossups.r: That woman, Eve, later uneasily recalls the dream to her husband, Adam. For 10 points, name this epic poem in which Satan first tries to corrupt Eve through her dreams.

tossups.p: Flattering this poem’s heroine with claims that a certain fruit grants godlike knowledge, a disguised villain convinces her to eat from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil. Her husband, though warned in advance, eats the same fruit anyway rather than face life without her.
tossups.r: Both then feel shame over their nakedness for the first time and begin to quarrel. For 10 points, name this epic poem about the Fall of Adam and Eve.

tossups.p: An archangel shows this poem’s first man a vision of future human history, including Cain’s murder of Abel and Noah’s flood, from a tall hill. That archangel then prepares to lead the man and his wife out of their garden home forever.
tossups.r: That archangel, Michael, offers comfort by promising a future savior despite humanity’s fall. For 10 points, name this epic poem that ends with Adam and Eve’s expulsion from Eden.

tossups.p: Cherubim bearing a flaming sword descend to seal off this poem’s garden forever as its two central characters look back at it in tears. An archangel takes each of them by the hand and leads them down to the plain below.
tossups.r: “The world was all before them,” Milton writes, as the couple sets off “with wandering steps and slow.” For 10 points, name this epic poem that ends with Adam and Eve’s expulsion from the Garden of Eden.

tossups.p: An archangel visits this poem’s garden to warn its first man about a looming danger, recounting both the six-day Creation of the universe and a great war fought in Heaven. That angel, Raphael, dines with Adam and Eve on fruit before launching into his long account.
tossups.r: His warning fails to stop a disguised villain from later tempting Eve. For 10 points, name this epic poem in which the angel Raphael tries to prepare Adam for Satan’s temptation.

tossups.p: This poem opens by invoking a “Heav’nly Muse” and announcing its subject as “Man’s first disobedience.” Its author defended its unrhymed form in a preface, calling rhyme “the invention of a barbarous age.”
tossups.r: That form, blank verse, let the poem’s long sentences unfold without the constraint of end rhyme. For 10 points, name this unrhymed epic poem by John Milton.

tossups.p: First published in 1667 in ten books, this poem was expanded to twelve books — matching the structure of Virgil’s _Aeneid_ — in a 1674 edition. Its author, totally blind by the time he composed it, dictated the entire poem aloud to a series of assistants.
tossups.r: That author also defended England’s execution of King Charles I in prose pamphlets. For 10 points, name this epic about Satan’s fall and humanity’s temptation, written by the blind poet John Milton.

tossups.p: This poem compares its fallen angels, lying stunned on a burning lake, to scattered autumn leaves, and later compares them thronging into their new capital to swarms of bees. That capital is built in a single hour using gold mined from the ground by the demon Mammon.
tossups.r: Its villain then calls a council there to plan revenge on Heaven. For 10 points, name this epic poem whose fallen angels regroup in Hell after their defeat.

tossups.p: Returning triumphantly to Hell after his first scheme succeeds, this poem’s villain is briefly transformed into a hissing serpent along with all his followers, forced to crawl toward fruit that turns to ashes in their mouths. This punishment repeats annually as a reminder of his crime.
tossups.r: That crime was tempting a certain woman in a garden. For 10 points, name this epic poem in which Satan is repeatedly humiliated after corrupting Eve.

tossups.p: This poem’s heroine recalls once gazing admiringly at her own reflection in a pool of water until a divine voice led her away to meet her husband instead. She was formed from a rib taken from that husband’s side while he slept.
tossups.r: Centuries of readers have compared that reflection scene to the Greek myth of Narcissus. For 10 points, name this epic poem whose heroine, Eve, is tempted by Satan soon after her creation.

tossups.p: This poem’s narrator states that his purpose is to “justify the ways of God to men.” Modeled on classical epics by Homer and Virgil, it tells a Christian story instead of a Greek or Roman one, opening in the middle of the action with its villain already defeated and bound in chains of fire.
tossups.r: Its true hero, if it even has one, might be Christ, Adam, or even Satan — a question critics still debate. For 10 points, name this epic poem about the Fall of Man, written by John Milton.

clues.t: Epic poem by John Milton about Satan’s rebellion against God and the fall of Adam and Eve
Adam and Eve are expelled from the Garden of Eden for eating forbidden fruit
Satan declares it is “Better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven”
Written in blank verse (unrhymed iambic pentameter), a bold choice for an English epic
Milton’s stated purpose, in his own words, was to “justify the ways of God to men”
Satan’s followers build Pandemonium, their new capital city in Hell
Archangel Michael shows Adam a vision of future human history, then leads the couple out of Eden
In Hell’s council, the demons Belial, Moloch, and Mammon argue over whether to make war again or scheme instead
Disguised as a serpent, Satan tempts Eve with fruit from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil
The Son of God single-handedly routs Satan’s armies to end the War in Heaven
First published in 1667 in ten books; Milton, totally blind, had dictated the whole poem aloud
Cherubim with a flaming sword guard Eden’s gate as Adam and Eve leave hand in hand
Opens with an invocation of a “Heav’nly Muse” and the line “Of Man’s first disobedience”
The monstrous Sin and Death guard Hell’s gates; Sin, Satan’s own daughter, lets him pass through
Disguised as a young cherub, Satan tricks the angel Uriel into pointing him toward Earth; he later perches on a tree in Eden like a cormorant
Satan travels through the formless realm of Chaos to reach the newly created universe
Disguised as a toad, Satan whispers a troubling dream into the sleeping Eve’s ear, but is caught by the angels Ithuriel and Zephon
The angel Raphael visits Eden to recount the six-day Creation and the War in Heaven as a warning
Mammon argues the fallen angels should mine Hell’s gold instead of fighting Heaven again
Knowing the consequences, Adam eats the forbidden fruit anyway rather than live without Eve
After the Fall, Satan and his followers are briefly turned into hissing serpents as punishment
Epic similes compare the fallen angels to scattered autumn leaves and, as they throng into their new capital, to swarms of bees
Expanded from ten to twelve books in a 1674 edition, echoing the structure of Virgil’s _Aeneid_

trap.title: Lost, or Regained?
trap.body: Milton wrote a much shorter sequel called _Paradise Regained_ (1671), about Christ resisting Satan’s temptation in the wilderness — a victory, not a fall. It is a completely different poem with a completely different plot, and real QBReader tossups never accept it for this answer line.
trap.fix: If the clues are about Satan’s rebellion, the War in Heaven, or Adam and Eve being cast out of Eden, it’s Paradise Lost. If the clues are about Christ resisting temptation in the desert, that is the sequel, Paradise Regained — reject it here.

topics.name: Nineteen Eighty-Four
topics.kicker: Orwell’s totalitarian nightmare · Gave English the word “Orwellian”
topics.briefing: George Orwell imagined a future where the government, led by the shadowy Big Brother, controls not just what people do but what they’re allowed to think. Winston Smith secretly rebels against the all-seeing Party by falling in love and keeping a secret diary, in a world of telescreens, Newspeak, and doublethink. _Nineteen Eighty-Four_ has haunted readers — and politics — ever since it was published in 1949.

tossups.p: This novel’s protagonist is finally broken in Room 101 when his interrogator straps a wire cage full of hungry rats toward his face, the one thing he fears most in the world. He saves himself only by screaming for the torment to be turned on someone he loves instead.
tossups.r: That interrogator, O’Brien, had posed as a member of a secret resistance movement. For 10 points, name this dystopian novel about Winston Smith’s rebellion against a totalitarian party, written by George Orwell.

tossups.p: Citizens in this novel are watched at all times through two-way telescreens that can never be fully turned off, even at home. Suspicious behavior like an unusual facial expression, called facecrime, can draw the attention of the regime’s secret police.
tossups.r: That secret police, the Thought Police, arrests anyone suspected of disloyal thoughtcrime. For 10 points, name this novel about constant government surveillance in the superstate of Oceania.

tossups.p: This novel’s totalitarian party is slowly replacing Standard English with a stripped-down official language designed to make rebellious thoughts almost impossible to express. A character helping compile that language’s dictionary is abruptly erased from existence, becoming an “unperson.”
tossups.r: That language, Newspeak, aims to shrink the range of human thought by shrinking vocabulary itself. For 10 points, name this novel that also coined the term “doublethink.”

tossups.p: This novel’s characters practice holding two contradictory beliefs at once and sincerely accepting both, a mental skill its ruling party calls doublethink. Party slogans built on this same contradiction declare that “War Is Peace” and “Freedom Is Slavery.”
tossups.r: The party’s third slogan, “Ignorance Is Strength,” completes the trio. For 10 points, name this novel in which the Party controls thought itself through doublethink and Newspeak.

tossups.p: This novel’s protagonist works in the Records Department of the Ministry of Truth, rewriting old newspaper articles so that history always matches the Party’s current claims. Outdated documents are dropped down a chute called a memory hole to be incinerated.
tossups.r: Yet he secretly rebels by keeping a forbidden diary. For 10 points, name this novel about Winston Smith’s work erasing inconvenient facts for a totalitarian government.

tossups.p: This novel’s protagonist buys an old coral-and-glass paperweight from a junk shop run by a man named Mr Charrington. He later rents a room above that same shop to secretly meet a woman he has fallen in love with.
tossups.r: That shop turns out to be a trap run by the Thought Police all along. For 10 points, name this novel in which a hidden telescreen eventually exposes Winston and Julia’s affair.

tossups.p: This novel’s heroine openly wears the sash of the Junior Anti-Sex League while secretly breaking nearly every rule the Party sets for personal behavior. She first slips the protagonist a note reading “I love you” after stumbling in a hallway at work.
tossups.r: She and the protagonist, Winston, begin a secret affair that the Party treats as a political crime. For 10 points, name this novel in which Julia and Winston are eventually betrayed and arrested.

tossups.p: This novel’s protagonist trusts an Inner Party member who claims to belong to a resistance group called the Brotherhood, supposedly led by the shadowy traitor Emmanuel Goldstein. That member lends him a banned book about the Party’s true strategy.
tossups.r: The member, O’Brien, turns out to be a loyal agent who has been watching the protagonist for years. For 10 points, name this novel in which Winston is entrapped by the Party loyalist O’Brien.

tossups.p: This novel’s world is permanently divided among three warring superstates: Oceania, Eurasia, and Eastasia. During an annual Hate Week rally, the identity of Oceania’s enemy abruptly switches mid-speech, and the crowd instantly accepts the Party’s new version of history.
tossups.r: No one in the crowd dares question this sudden, obvious contradiction. For 10 points, name this novel set in Airstrip One, a province of the superstate Oceania.

tossups.p: This novel’s protagonist lives in Victory Mansions, next door to a fanatically loyal Party man named Parsons. Parsons is eventually denounced to the Thought Police and arrested after his own young daughter overhears him talking in his sleep.
tossups.r: That daughter belongs to the Spies, a youth group trained to inform on its own parents. For 10 points, name this novel about a surveillance state where even families can’t be trusted.

tossups.p: The lowest class in this novel, the proles, are left largely unwatched by the Party and allowed beer, pulp films, and a weekly National Lottery as a kind of pressure valve. This novel’s protagonist sometimes wonders whether real rebellion could only ever come from that class.
tossups.r: He studies the proles hopefully but never finds the resistance movement he’s looking for. For 10 points, name this novel about Winston Smith’s doomed search for freedom in a totalitarian state.

tossups.p: Strapped into a device that causes him pain whenever he answers incorrectly, this novel’s protagonist is slowly made to agree that two plus two can equal five, if the Party says so. His interrogator insists that the Party’s control of reality itself is absolute.
tossups.r: That interrogator, O’Brien, later sends him to Room 101 to finish breaking his spirit completely. For 10 points, name this novel about the limits of objective truth under a totalitarian party.

tossups.p: This novel opens, “It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen.” A minor character named Syme, who works on a dictionary of the Party’s official language, later disappears from work without warning.
tossups.r: Syme has simply become an “unperson,” erased from every record as though he never existed. For 10 points, name this novel, which ends with its broken protagonist finally deciding that he loves Big Brother.

tossups.p: This novel’s protagonist repeatedly dreams of a peaceful, sunlit landscape he calls the Golden Country, which turns out to match a real field where he later meets his lover in secret. He also has fragmented memories of his mother and sister vanishing when he was a boy.
tossups.r: Those hazy childhood memories predate the Party’s full takeover of his country. For 10 points, name this novel narrated from inside the mind of Winston Smith.

tossups.p: This novel’s government runs four ironically named Ministries: the Ministry of Truth handles propaganda, the Ministry of Peace handles war, the Ministry of Plenty handles rationing and scarcity, and the Ministry of Love handles torture and interrogation.
tossups.r: Each Ministry’s real function is the exact opposite of its cheerful name. For 10 points, name this novel set in a totalitarian superstate ruled by Big Brother and the Party.

clues.t: Dystopian novel by George Orwell about a totalitarian superstate called Oceania
Protagonist Winston Smith works at the Ministry of Truth, rewriting history to fit the Party’s lies
The Party is led by the all-seeing, possibly fictional figurehead Big Brother
Citizens are watched through two-way telescreens and the Thought Police
Party slogans include “War Is Peace” and “Freedom Is Slavery”
Winston is tortured in Room 101 of the Ministry of Love, where prisoners face their own worst fear
Winston’s lover Julia secretly meets him above Mr Charrington’s antique shop
O’Brien pretends to belong to a resistance group called the Brotherhood, supposedly led by Emmanuel Goldstein
Winston is finally broken by his worst fear — rats — and betrays Julia to save himself
In his secret diary, Winston writes the forbidden words “DOWN WITH BIG BROTHER” over and over
The Party’s constructed language, Newspeak, is designed to make rebellious thoughts impossible to even express
Doublethink lets Party members sincerely hold two contradictory beliefs at once
Winston works in the Records Department, dropping inconvenient documents down a “memory hole”
Interrogated until he agrees that “two plus two makes five” if the Party says so
Goldstein’s banned book, _The Theory and Practice of Oligarchical Collectivism_, explains the Party’s real strategy
Oceania is one of three endlessly warring superstates, alongside Eurasia and Eastasia
During Hate Week, the enemy nation switches mid-speech and the crowd instantly accepts the new version of history
Julia openly wears the sash of the Junior Anti-Sex League while secretly breaking its rules
Neighbor Parsons is denounced to the Thought Police by his own fanatical child
Buys an old coral-and-glass paperweight from Mr Charrington’s shop
A coworker named Syme, who helps compile the Newspeak dictionary, is abruptly “vaporized” into an unperson
The novel opens, “It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen”
Ends with its broken protagonist finally deciding that he loves Big Brother

trap.title: The novel, or its dictator?
trap.body: “Big Brother” is the Party’s all-seeing figurehead inside the story — not the title of the book. Kids (and plenty of adults) mix them up constantly. Winston Smith is the hero, not the title either, and George Orwell is the author, who also wrote a very different dystopia, Animal Farm.
trap.fix: If the question asks you to “name this novel” or “name this work,” the answer is Nineteen Eighty-Four (or 1984), not Big Brother, Winston Smith, or George Orwell — and not Animal Farm, which is a totally different book by the same author.
